title: Microsoft Tightens Oversight of AI Data Center Partners Following $5B Capex Gap

tickers.name: Nebius Group N.V. Class A Ordinary Shares

summary:
The cloud provider has revised its strategy for partnering with smaller data center developers, abandoning several high-risk deals and implementing stricter audits of construction progress. This change in approach follows reporting that Microsoft spent roughly $5B less on planned infrastructure in the third quarter due to delays from "neocloud" providers such as Iren, Nebius, and Nscale. Recent satellite imagery from research firm Aterio highlights missing backup generators at Iren's Horizon 4 facility in Texas, while generator and fuel-cell permitting delays may push a Nebius project in New Jersey into 2027.

In response to these technical hurdles, Iren is shifting its funding model to have customers absorb more buildout costs to avoid further equity dilution. A new five-year contract at approximately $22M per megawatt now requires the client to prepay 90% of GPU capital expenditures, while a separate short-term deal was signed at $40M per megawatt. Despite these agreements and a $20.3B revenue backlog, Iren reported a $263M net loss for its September quarter, with revenue of $228M and a target for $4B in annualized revenue pushed to early 2027 following a network redesign request from Microsoft.

JUST IN: Microsoft cut its annual AI capital spending forecast by $5B after third-party data center delays. Satellite analysis suggests projects tied to IREN ($IREN) and Nebius ($NBIS), worth $27.1B combined, may be contributing.

October 21 satellite images showed missing backup generators and cooling equipment at Horizon 4, one of four Texas facilities $IREN owns, raising concerns about its year-end deadline. Horizon 1 was previously delayed by equipment shortages but accepted in August.

Research firm Aterio estimates roughly 140 MW at $NBIS New Jersey project could slip into 2027 following generator and fuel-cell permitting delays. Developer DataOne was fined $1M in September for operating generators without permits.

selectedTweets.text:
$IREN just reported earnings and there are some HUGE developments here that I think investors are overlooking.

Revenue came in at $228M, beating expectations of $221M, with AI Cloud revenue accounting for $200M. The company also reported an impressive 86% gross margin in its AI Cloud business but the biggest news is what they're doing with their contracts.

IREN now has a $20.3B revenue backlog, with roughly two thirds coming from investment grade counterparties. Management also announced a new five-year contract worth approximately $22M per megawatt, with the customer prepaying 90% of the GPU capital expenditures. They also signed a short-term contract worth $40M per megawatt. That's a pretty big deal because one of the biggest concerns surrounding neoclouds has been how they're going to finance their enormous AI infrastructure buildouts without constantly raising capital or taking on additional debt. Having customers cover 90% of GPU capex significantly reduces that funding burden.

The downside is that IREN still reported a $263M net loss, has another $15B in planned FY27 capex, and its $4B+ contracted ARR target has been pushed into January, potentially February, due to design changes and supplier timing. I still think the bigger picture here is extremely interesting. AI infrastructure demand clearly remains strong, customers are willing to commit billions of dollars years in advance, and IREN is finding ways to shift some of the financial burden directly onto those customers.The question now is whether they can execute on that enormous backlog without running into further delays or funding issues.
